name: Bench press
angleNote: Bar height: 0% = on the chest, 100% = arms locked out. Torques are per arm; drag the figure to turn it.
momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the bar's push line through that hand; it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

joints.name: Shoulder (across)
joints.angleLabel: upper-arm angle (0° = out to the side, 90° = up)

strength.note: Relative horizontal-adduction strength vs arm angle (0° = arms out in line with the shoulders): constant from 30° behind that line to 60° in front, then a sharp drop (Williams & Stutzman, 10 men; Whitley, 31 men, found no change over 60°; both via Kulig et al.). How far it drops by 90–120° isn't given numerically, so those values are estimates. Peak per arm: Lategan's mean horizontal-adduction torque for men, 92 ± 23 Nm (isokinetic, 60°/s, not gravity-corrected).
strength.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape; drop beyond 60° estimated); peak: Lategan L (2002). Normative isokinetic torque values for rehabilitation in South Africa. DPhil thesis, University of Pretoria, Table 6.17 (103 men aged 16–29, isokinetic 60°/s, concentric, lying on the back with the arm out at 90°, not gravity-corrected). https://repository.up.ac.za/handle/2263/27346

strength.note: Relative shoulder-flexion strength vs the upper arm's elevation from the trunk (as in the overhead press; on an incline the arm works further overhead): "descending" in all three studies Kulig et al. reviewed, strongest low, with a plateau around 45–90° and a clear drop only beyond about 110°. The size of the drop across 0–90° isn't given numerically, so these values are an estimate of that shape; Mayer et al. found the isometric peak at 35–72° (men). Peak torque default: Mayer's isometric shoulder flexion, men, 68 ± 18 Nm. From 90° to 160° the drop is measured: standing isometric shoulder flexion fell almost linearly, to 56% of its 90° value at 160° (Aronis et al., Table 1); the points here are those ratios applied to the 90° value, held flat beyond 160° (not measured). Their mean at 90° was 77 Nm including the arm's own weight, above this curve's 63 Nm there; the default peak stays at Mayer's value.
strength.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape); Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105 (peak torque); above 110°: TODO, no source checked for the size of the drop; Aronis G, Kurz M, Wimmer F, Hackl H, Angeli T, Gföhler M (2025). Maximum shoulder torque and muscle activation during standing arm flexion: reference data for biomechanical and ergonomic applications. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010020 (14 men, standing, isometric, 90–160° every 10°; Table 1 torque, Table 2 EMG)

strength.note: Relative shoulder-abduction strength vs abduction: strongest at 30°, weakest with the arm by the side (0°). From a conference abstract (hand-held myometer, 30 adults): +31.3% at 30°, +12.5% at 60° and −18.8% at 0° relative to 90°; Mayer et al. 1994 place the isometric peak at 27–65° in men. The weakest evidence of the curves here. Peak torque default: Mayer's isometric shoulder abduction, men, 47 ± 12 Nm. The sources disagree near the start: Clarke et al. (64 men, supine, via Kulig et al.) found abduction strongest with the arm by the side and a plateau at 45–90°. Treat the 0–30° part as uncertain. Above 90° the curve here is an estimate (50% at 180°). Adduction peak (90 Nm) is also an estimate.
strength.source: Haidar SG, Lloyd J, Cox D, Deshmukh S (2009). Shoulder abduction strength: is it affected by the degree of abduction? J Bone Joint Surg Br 91-B Suppl I:160 (conference abstract). doi:10.1302/0301-620X.91BSUPP_I.0910160c; Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Normal values of isokinetic maximum strength, the strength/velocity curve, and the angle at peak torque of all degrees of freedom in the shoulder. Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105; Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (Clarke et al., contrary finding at 0°); above 90° and the adduction peak: TODO, no source checked

strength.note: Shoulder external (positive) and internal (negative) rotation peak torque per arm, taken as constant: Mayer's isometric means for men (30 and 43 Nm).
strength.source: Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25, Table 2 (men, dominant side, isometric)

strength.note: Relative isometric elbow-extension torque vs elbow flexion (0° = straight), peak about 55°: the paper's mean cubic fit, normalised, inside the measured 20–116° (held flat beyond). Measured with the upper arm raised 90° to the side, so the long head's length differs from overhead or arm-at-side positions. Peak per arm: the paper's male mean, 77 Nm (rounded to 80 for trained lifters).
strength.source: Pinter IJ, Bobbert MF, van Soest AJ, Smeets JBJ (2010). Isometric torque–angle relationships of the elbow flexors and extensors in the transverse plane. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 20:923–931. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2010.05.001

strength.note: No muscle capacity: the elbow's sideways moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

muscles.name: Pectoralis major
muscles.note: Main horizontal adductor. Measured: wider grips raise the shoulder's moment and the abdominal head's EMG; the sternocostal head barely changes (Mausehund et al.). Same in barbell, dumbbell and Smith-machine presses (Saeterbakken et al.). Inclining the bench moves work from the sternal to the clavicular head: the sternal head falls at every incline, the clavicular head rises at 44–56° but not at 28° (Trebs et al.).
muscles.source: Grip-width effect: Mausehund L, Werkhausen A, Bartsch J, Krosshaug T (2022). Understanding bench press biomechanics — the necessity of measuring lateral barbell forces. J Strength Cond Res 36(10):2685–2695; Saeterbakken AH, van den Tillaar R, Fimland MS (2011). A comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements. J Sports Sci 29(5):533–538. doi:10.1080/02640414.2010.543916 (12 trained men, 1RM lifts); Trebs AA, Brandenburg JP, Pitney WA (2010). An electromyography analysis of 3 muscles surrounding the shoulder joint during the performance of a chest press exercise at several angles. J Strength Cond Res 24(7):1925–1930. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddfae7 (15 men, 70% 1RM, Smith machine; values in figures only)

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Shoulder flexor; also helps horizontal adduction, and on an incline holds the arm against being pulled towards the feet (abduction), taking the larger demand. Higher at every incline than flat (Trebs et al.); 21% of maximum at 60% 1RM flat, with the middle and rear deltoid at 5% and 3.5% (Campos et al.).
muscles.source: Trebs AA, Brandenburg JP, Pitney WA (2010). An electromyography analysis of 3 muscles surrounding the shoulder joint during the performance of a chest press exercise at several angles. J Strength Cond Res 24(7):1925–1930. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddfae7 (15 men, 70% 1RM, Smith machine; values in figures only); Campos YAC, Vianna JM, Guimarães MP, Oliveira JLD, Hernández-Mosqueira C, da Silva SF, Marchetti PH (2020). Different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals. J Hum Kinet 75:5–14. doi:10.2478/hukin-2020-0033 (13 men, 60% 1RM, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Triceps
muscles.note: Elbow extensor. Measured: narrower grips raise the elbow's moment (by up to 26%) and the lateral head's EMG (Mausehund et al.). This model's elbow moment arm (15–20 cm) is about twice the measured one (7–9 cm), so its triceps numbers run high. Lower with dumbbells than a barbell (Saeterbakken et al.).
muscles.source: Grip-width effect and moment arms: Mausehund L, Werkhausen A, Bartsch J, Krosshaug T (2022). Understanding bench press biomechanics — the necessity of measuring lateral barbell forces. J Strength Cond Res 36(10):2685–2695; Saeterbakken AH, van den Tillaar R, Fimland MS (2011). A comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements. J Sports Sci 29(5):533–538. doi:10.1080/02640414.2010.543916 (12 trained men, 1RM lifts)

muscles.name: Infraspinatus, teres minor
muscles.note: External rotators of the rotator cuff: hold the upper arm from turning inwards.

muscles.name: Subscapularis
muscles.note: Internal rotator of the rotator cuff: holds the upper arm from turning outwards.

phases.name: Off the chest
phases.text: Bar on the chest, furthest in front of the shoulder: the shoulder's largest moment arm.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The bar moves back over the shoulder as it rises.

phases.name: Lockout
phases.text: Bar over the shoulders: little shoulder torque; whatever the elbows still do depends on the grip.

variants.name: Flat bench, medium grip
variants.notes: Medium grip. Grip width from Mausehund et al.'s arm–bar angle at lockout (75°), converted with this model's arm length and shoulder width; touch point from their measured shoulder moment arm at the bottom; chest raised 20 cm above the shoulder joints for the arch (their arch angle was about 30°; the height is an estimate). Elbows as close under the bar as the arm allows (the shoulder joints stay put): this placement gives elbow moment arms close to the ones Mausehund et al. measured for the medium grip, too small for the wide grip and too large for the narrow one (see docs/model-limits.md). Each hand pushes up with half the bar by default. Lifters also pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow (try the bar-spread slider).

variants.name: Wide grip
variants.notes: Hands far out: the upper arms flare, the pecs (horizontal adduction) work much harder and the triceps less. The bar also travels less. Grip width from Mausehund et al.'s arm–bar angle at lockout (65°), converted with this model's arm length and shoulder width, touch point an estimate; chest raised 20 cm above the shoulder joints for the arch (their arch angle was about 30°; the height is an estimate). Elbows as close under the bar as the arm allows (the shoulder joints stay put): this placement gives elbow moment arms close to the ones Mausehund et al. measured for the medium grip, too small for the wide grip and too large for the narrow one (see docs/model-limits.md). Each hand pushes up with half the bar by default. Lifters also pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow (try the bar-spread slider).

variants.name: Close grip
variants.notes: Hands about shoulder width, elbows tucked, bar lower on the chest: the triceps take over and the pecs' across-the-body work nearly vanishes. Grip width from Mausehund et al.'s arm–bar angle at lockout (85°), converted with this model's arm length and shoulder width; touch point from their measured shoulder moment arm at the bottom; chest raised 20 cm above the shoulder joints for the arch (their arch angle was about 30°; the height is an estimate). Elbows as close under the bar as the arm allows (the shoulder joints stay put): this placement gives elbow moment arms close to the ones Mausehund et al. measured for the medium grip, too small for the wide grip and too large for the narrow one (see docs/model-limits.md). Each hand pushes up with half the bar by default. Lifters also pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow (try the bar-spread slider).

variants.name: Medium grip, elbows flared past the hands
variants.notes: Elbows pushed 6 cm outside the hands, no arch and the bar lowered high on the chest, near the neck: compare the rotation torque, the flare angle and the elbow's moment arm with the medium grip. Each hand pushes up with half the bar by default. Lifters also pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow (try the bar-spread slider).

variants.name: Incline bench (30°), medium grip
variants.notes: Bench tilted 30°: the bar touches the upper chest and presses vertically over the shoulders. Elbows as close under the bar as the arm allows. Each hand pushes up with half the bar by default. Lifters also pull the bar apart: Mausehund et al. measured a lateral force of about 17% of the vertical force with a medium grip, 38% wide and about 0% narrow (try the bar-spread slider).
